stem: An expert planner resists the new scheduling tool. What usually works best?

options.a: Escalate to the plant director so that tool usage is enforced from above
options.b: Move the planner off the project to avoid friction
options.c: Make the planner a co-author: encode their rules, show their data
options.d: Tie tool usage targets to the planner's bonus from day one

explanation: Resistance usually signals a fear, such as losing expertise or status. Turning the expert from suspect into co-author puts their rules in the model and their name on the result.
author: claude-spec

stem: Why reshuffle teams around a new AI asset, even when headcount is a small part of the gain?

options.a: An asset dropped into an unchanged organization gets absorbed by it
options.b: Payroll reduction is where most of the program's value really comes from
options.c: Employee representatives require a new organization chart
options.d: New roles make the program more visible to the board

explanation: The reshuffle is not the gain; it is what makes the other gain lines reachable. Unchanged teams keep taking yesterday's decisions with today's tool.
author: claude-spec

stem: What does the history of factory electrification teach about AI adoption?

options.a: Early adopters capture most of the value
options.b: Gains came once work was redesigned and a new generation trained
options.c: Adoption only takes off once the cost of the technology has collapsed
options.d: Regulation is the main driver of adoption

explanation: Electric motors paid off decades after they arrived, once factories were redesigned around them (Paul David). Plan the redesign, and overweight training for the incoming generation.
author: claude-spec

stem: Operators override the scheduler's plan 30% of the time. What should the FDE do first?

options.a: Lock the plan in the system so that operators can no longer change it at all
options.b: Send the operators back through the training program
options.c: Report low adoption of the tool to the project sponsor
options.d: Study the reasons: each override points to a missing rule or bad data

explanation: Overrides are information. Each reveals a constraint the model lacks or data that is wrong; fixing them is how trust and accuracy rise together.
author: claude-spec

stem: Two weeks after go-live at Polymex Industries, schedule adherence is below its old level. The plant manager wants to roll back. What do you advise?

options.a: Roll back now and relaunch the tool once the whole team has been retrained
options.b: Hold course: a dip before the rise was expected and planned for
options.c: Enforce the tool through daily usage KPIs so adherence recovers fast
options.d: Accept that the planners' old method was better and keep it

explanation: Performance dips before it rises on the change curve; the plan should have budgeted for it. Rolling back at the dip throws away the change just before it pays.
author: claude

stem: Go-live is planned for March. What should the plan include for the performance dip expected in the first weeks?

options.a: Targets raised early, to push the team through the dip faster
options.b: A rollback to the old method at the first drop in output
options.c: Buffers in targets and capacity, plus extra support on the floor
options.d: A message to the floor that results will improve from the first day

explanation: On the change curve, performance dips before it rises. Planning buffers and support for the dip keeps it from being read as failure and triggering a rollback.
author: claude

stem: Planners have stopped arguing against the new tool and now try it on a few orders, asking many questions. Which stage of the change curve is this?

options.a: Denial
options.b: Resistance
options.c: Exploration
options.d: Commitment

explanation: The curve runs denial, resistance, exploration, commitment. Trying the tool and asking questions is exploration; support matters most here.
author: claude

stem: A quality lead raises a new technical objection each time the previous one is answered. What is the most likely reading?

options.a: The tool has deep technical flaws that the project team has missed
options.b: The quality lead is being irrational and is best kept away from the project
options.c: The objections call for a longer written answer from the vendor
options.d: A fear, such as losing status or being blamed, drives the objections

explanation: Resistance usually signals a fear: status, expertise, job or blame. When answers do not end objections, the argument is not the real issue; address the fear.
author: claude

stem: Senior planners fear the tool will be used to blame them for late orders. Which response addresses this best?

options.a: Agree openly how plan errors will be reviewed, as a team and without blame
options.b: Show benchmark data proving that the tool's plans beat the plans they make by hand today
options.c: Promise them that tool usage will not be monitored in any way
options.d: Escalate to the sponsor so the concern does not slow the project

explanation: Address the fear, not only the argument. Accuracy data answers the argument but leaves the fear of blame intact.
author: claude

stem: During co-authoring, an expert planner's sequencing rule contradicts the ERP data. What should the team do?

options.a: Keep the ERP version, since it is the official system of record
options.b: Encode the rule as stated, without checking, to keep the expert on side
options.c: Test the rule with the expert on real cases, then encode it if it holds
options.d: Drop the rule to keep the model simple until after go-live

explanation: Co-authorship means the expert's rules go into the model, checked against real cases. Ignoring them loses the rule and the expert; encoding them blindly loses accuracy.
author: claude

stem: The tool will soon publish plans built on rules from the plant's best planner. Why put that planner's name on the result?

options.a: It makes the planner formally accountable, in writing, for each plan the tool issues from now on
options.b: It gives the planner ownership, so they defend the tool instead of attacking it
options.c: It lets management compare the planner's output with colleagues' output
options.d: It shows the vendor which users should be trained first

explanation: Experts become co-authors: their rules in the model, their name on the result. The suspect becomes the author, with a stake in the tool's success.
author: claude

stem: The project team leaves in three months. Who should carry the tool afterward?

options.a: The IT helpdesk, which already supports every other application running in the plant today
options.b: The vendor's customer success manager, through quarterly calls
options.c: Whichever planner happens to use the tool the most, informally
options.d: An internal operational champion with a formal role and legitimacy

explanation: An internal operational champion with a formal role, legitimacy and a direct line to the software teams carries the tools after the project team leaves.
author: claude

stem: Noor volunteers to be the tool's champion, on top of her full planning job, with no title or time set aside. What is missing?

options.a: Nothing: volunteering shows the motivation a champion needs most
options.b: A deeper technical background so she can change the code herself
options.c: A formal role and the legitimacy to speak for the floor
options.d: A bonus tied to the number of tool logins on her team

explanation: Goodwill is not enough. The champion needs a formal role and legitimacy, plus a direct line to the software teams, to keep the tool alive after the project ends.
author: claude

stem: Why should the tool's champion usually come from operations rather than from IT?

options.a: Peers on the floor trust someone who knows their work and its constraints
options.b: IT staff are not allowed to change production schedules or planning data in most plants
options.c: Operations staff need much less training on the software itself
options.d: IT will be busy with integration work for years after go-live

explanation: The champion is operational: legitimacy with the people who use the tool daily is what carries it. IT remains a partner, reached through the champion's direct line.
author: claude

stem: A champion's direct line to the software team matters mainly because:

options.a: It lets the champion bypass the plant's IT security rules
options.b: Floor needs reach the people who can change the tool, quickly
options.c: It replaces the need for a steering committee after go-live
options.d: The software team can then monitor each user's activity in detail

explanation: Without a direct line, requests from the floor stall and the tool falls behind the work. The champion turns floor needs into changes.
author: claude

stem: The new tool now does sequencing that took two planners all day. Which reshuffle fits the course?

options.a: Keep both planners in their old roles to avoid disruption on the floor
options.b: Remove both planner positions at once to book the payroll saving
options.c: Let each planner decide individually how to use the time that was freed
options.d: Redesign their roles around exceptions and capacity decisions the tool surfaces

explanation: An asset dropped into an unchanged organization gets absorbed by it. Redesigning roles around the new work is what makes the other gain lines reachable.
author: claude

stem: The CEO wants to announce the AI program at next week's all-hands, before the first tool works. What do you advise?

options.a: Build quietly until it demonstrably works, then reveal it
options.b: Announce it now so that every employee has plenty of time to prepare for it
options.c: Announce now, and promise that no role will ever change
options.d: Announce only the budget and keep the scope confidential

explanation: Build in silence until the asset demonstrably works. An early announcement invites fears and rumors with nothing yet to show.
author: claude

stem: The tool is ready to be shown to the whole plant. Besides the tool itself, what should the presentation include?

options.a: A live demo, with the rest of the details to follow in later months
options.b: The vendor's roadmap of upcoming features and releases
options.c: The usage targets each planner must hit from the first week
options.d: The capture plan, the new team organization and the training

explanation: The reveal comes as a package: the working asset, the capture plan, the new team and the training. A demo alone leaves people guessing what changes for them.
author: claude

stem: The training budget for a new planning tool is limited. Where does the course suggest putting extra weight?

options.a: On the most senior staff, who have the most habits to unlearn
options.b: On managers, who can then cascade the training to their teams
options.c: On one go-live session that covers everyone at the same time
options.d: On the incoming generation who will run the redesigned work

explanation: Electrification paid off once work was redesigned and a new generation trained. Overweight training for the people who will carry the new way of working for decades.
author: claude

stem: A project plan treats change management as a two-day training at go-live. What is wrong with it?

options.a: Two days is too short; it should be a full week of classroom training
options.b: Change runs through the whole project, starting at scoping
options.c: Nothing, provided the training covers every feature of the tool
options.d: Training should be left to the vendor to save time for the project team

explanation: Change management is not training at the end. It runs through the project: experts as co-authors, a champion, a reshuffled team, a planned reveal.
author: claude

stem: A year after go-live, planners are back on spreadsheets; the tool still runs on its original rules. What was most likely missing?

options.a: A strict mandate that blocks the use of spreadsheets for planning on the plant network
options.b: A second round of go-live training for every planner
options.c: A regular feedback loop where the client says how its needs changed
options.d: An upgrade to the latest model release from the vendor

explanation: Needs change after go-live. Without regular moments where the client says what changed, tools decay on autopilot and people drift back to their own workarounds.
author: claude

stem: Camille, an expert scheduler, fears that once her rules are in the tool she will no longer be needed. What addresses this best?

options.a: Being clear early about her role after go-live, built on her expertise
options.b: Showing her that the tool's plans are already more accurate than her own
options.c: Postponing the question until after go-live to avoid tension now
options.d: Telling her that questions about jobs are outside the project's scope

explanation: Resistance usually signals a fear, here for her job. Address the fear itself; proving the tool better than her answers the argument and sharpens the fear.
author: claude

stem: While a tool is built in silence, who outside the core project team should know about it?

options.a: The sponsor and the experts who co-author the model
options.b: Nobody at all, the expert planners included, until the reveal
options.c: The whole plant, through a regular project newsletter
options.d: Only the vendor, since it supplies the software

explanation: Building in silence means no public announcement before the asset works, not secrecy from the sponsor or from the experts whose rules go into the model.
author: claude

stem: How should you describe the scheduling tool's goal to the shop floor?

options.a: In headcount terms: how many planning hours the plant can now cut
options.b: In throughput terms: more good output from the same lines
options.c: In technical terms: the model and data platform behind it
options.d: In cost terms: the euro savings finance expects each year

explanation: Communicate in throughput terms. Headcount framing feeds the job fear behind resistance; technical framing means little to the people affected.
author: claude

stem: Employee representatives must be consulted on new work tools at your site. When should you involve them?

options.a: Early, as required, before the rollout is already decided
options.b: After go-live, once the results of the tool can speak for themselves
options.c: Only if staff raise a formal complaint about the tool
options.d: At the public reveal, at the same time as everyone else

explanation: Where consultation is required, involve representatives early. Bringing them in after decisions are made turns a formal step into a conflict.
author: claude

stem: IT has blocked the tool's network access for three weeks and the team cannot resolve it. Whose job is it to remove the blocker?

options.a: The steering committee's, at its next scheduled meeting
options.b: The champion's, through informal contacts within IT
options.c: The sponsor's, who has the authority to clear it now
options.d: The vendor account manager's, through their IT contacts

explanation: The sponsor removes blockers; the steering committee keeps the cadence. Waiting for the next committee lets a three-week block become a two-month one.
author: claude

stem: In a deployment, what is the main job of the steering committee?

options.a: Remove day-to-day blockers as soon as they come up on site, without waiting
options.b: Approve each change to the tool's code before it ships
options.c: Stand in for the sponsor whenever the sponsor is unavailable
options.d: Keep the cadence: regular reviews of progress, issues and decisions

explanation: The steering committee keeps the cadence; the sponsor removes blockers. A committee that waits to clear daily blockers is too slow for them.
author: claude

stem: Which signal best shows that a planning team has reached commitment on the change curve?

options.a: Logins have risen every week since go-live, on all shifts and all lines
options.b: Planners propose improvements and defend the tool to peers
options.c: Complaints about the tool have stopped since it went live
options.d: Every planner has completed the full training course

explanation: Commitment shows in ownership: people improve the tool and stand up for it. Silence, logins and training records can coexist with quiet resistance.
author: claude

stem: The override log shows planners always move one order type off line 2 on night shift. What does this most likely reveal?

options.a: Night-shift planners need refresher training on how to use the tool's plans
options.b: A missing constraint, such as a night-shift skill or tooling limit
options.c: The tool is right and the night shift is ignoring its plans
options.d: Random noise that will average out over the coming months

explanation: A systematic override points to a rule the model lacks or data that is wrong. Treating it as a training or discipline issue throws that information away.
author: claude

stem: When a user overrides a plan, what should the tool capture so the team can learn from it?

options.a: Only the count, so the override rate can be tracked over time
options.b: The user's name, so that repeat overriders can be retrained
options.c: Nothing, since logging overrides tends to discourage users
options.d: The changed decision plus a short, structured reason for it

explanation: Overrides are information only if their reasons are captured. A count shows the size of the problem, not which rule or data is missing.
author: claude

stem: The override rate fell from 30% to 5% in two months. What should the FDE check before celebrating?

options.a: That logins on the tool rose by the same proportion
options.b: That the sponsor has been told the tool is now trusted
options.c: That the drop came from fixed rules and data, not from users giving up
options.d: That the remaining overrides are spread evenly across all users and all shifts

explanation: Fewer overrides is good news only if missing rules and bad data were fixed. Users who stop overriding but decide elsewhere have abandoned the tool, not adopted it.
author: claude

stem: The vendor dashboard shows 95% daily logins. What better shows real adoption?

options.a: The average length of each user's session per day
options.b: The number of reports exported from the tool each week
options.c: The share of staff who completed the full training course on the tool
options.d: The share of decisions actually taken with the tool's plans

explanation: Adoption is not usage. Count decisions taken with the tool and the reasons for overrides; logins and sessions measure presence, not decisions.
author: claude

stem: Planners log in every morning, then build the actual plan in their own spreadsheet. How should the FDE read this?

options.a: Usage without adoption: find why decisions still happen outside the tool
options.b: Successful adoption, since every planner logs in to the tool daily
options.c: A training gap, best fixed with extra classroom sessions for every planner on site
options.d: A discipline problem, best fixed by blocking the spreadsheets

explanation: Logging in is not deciding. The spreadsheet holds rules or data the tool lacks, or a fear not yet addressed; finding which is the work.
author: claude

stem: Management wants to tie bonuses to tool login counts from day one. What is the likely effect?

options.a: Adoption rises, since the bonus gives every user a clear target
options.b: Resistance disappears once money is at stake for each user
options.c: Logins rise while real decisions keep being made elsewhere
options.d: Data quality improves because users enter more information

explanation: Mandating usage through KPIs from day one buys logins, not decisions. It also hides the override reasons that would improve the tool.
author: claude

stem: Alex, a respected shift leader, calls the new tool 'a toy'. Which first move does the course favor?

options.a: Ask his manager to add tool usage to his yearly objectives
options.b: Show him the vendor's case studies from other plants
options.c: Leave him out until the rest of the team is convinced
options.d: Use the tool to solve one of his daily pains first

explanation: To turn a skeptic, solve one of their pains first, show their own data and give them authorship. Mandates and outside case studies do not address why he doubts.
author: claude

stem: A skeptical quality lead doubts the tool's defect predictions. Which evidence is most likely to persuade her?

options.a: Accuracy figures from the vendor's benchmark at other plants
options.b: The predictions replayed on her own line's past batches
options.c: A demo on a clean sample dataset prepared by the team
options.d: Testimonials from users at a sister site of the group

explanation: Skeptics trust their own data. A replay on her line's history answers her doubt in her terms; benchmarks and clean demos invite the reply 'not here'.
author: claude

stem: Sam, the most skeptical planner, keeps finding errors in the tool's plans. How can the FDE best use this?

options.a: Make him the reviewer who writes the missing rules, credited by name
options.b: Limit his access to the tool so that his criticism does not spread
options.c: Collect his errors into a formal report for the software vendor
options.d: Ask him to hold his findings until the next scheduled release

explanation: Give the skeptic authorship. His error-finding is the best source of missing rules, and authorship turns the critic into a defender.
author: claude

stem: A maintenance lead objects that the tool ignores planned stops. You reply at once with accuracy statistics. What did you skip?

options.a: Confirming the objection with his manager before you replied
options.b: Sending the objection to the vendor for a formal answer
options.c: Acknowledging his concern and clarifying the case behind it
options.d: Waiting for the steering committee to rule on the objection

explanation: Objection handling runs acknowledge, clarify, answer with evidence, confirm. Statistics fired back unasked miss the specific case and make the person feel unheard.
author: claude

stem: A planner says the plans ignore a cleaning step on line 3. What is the strongest answer?

options.a: Overall accuracy figures showing that the tool performs well across all lines on average
options.b: Real plans showing whether the step is handled, or a fix if it is not
options.c: A promise that the vendor will look at it in a later release
options.d: An explanation that the cleaning step is a minor edge case

explanation: Answer with evidence on the specific case. If the objection is right, it is an override-style signal: fix the rule and show the fix.
author: claude

stem: You have answered a planner's objection about rush orders. What closes the loop?

options.a: Logging the objection as resolved in the project tracker
options.b: Reporting the outcome to her manager the same day
options.c: Moving on quickly so the meeting stays on schedule
options.d: Confirming with her that the answer resolves the concern

explanation: The last step is confirm: check with the person that the concern is resolved. Closing it on your own side leaves the objection alive on hers.
author: claude

stem: You must tell a production manager that his team's data entry causes most plan errors. How should you open?

options.a: With the facts: the error log and the cases traced to data entry
options.b: With your view that his team needs more discipline in data entry
options.c: With praise, keeping the problem for the end of the meeting
options.d: With a reminder that the sponsor expects results this quarter

explanation: Difficult conversations start with facts before opinions. The traced cases give him something to examine instead of a judgment to defend against.
author: claude

stem: In a tense review, a planner says the project 'is making him look incompetent'. Which reply follows the course?

options.a: Reassure him that the tool is right, so he has nothing at all to fear from it
options.b: Agree that some planners will struggle with the change
options.c: Separate him from the problem: the issue is the process, not his skill
options.d: End the meeting and report the conflict to the sponsor

explanation: Separate the person from the problem. Locating the issue in the process protects his standing and keeps the discussion on what to fix.
author: claude

stem: How should a difficult conversation with a resistant department head end?

options.a: On a summary of everything that has gone wrong so far
options.b: On an agreed next step, with an owner and a date
options.c: On a reminder of what the sponsor expects from the department
options.d: Without commitments, to let emotions settle for a while

explanation: End on a next step. Without an owner and a date, the conversation changes nothing on the ground.
author: claude

stem: A planner ignored a delay the tool had flagged, and a delivery was late. How should you raise it with him?

options.a: Start from the dated facts and look together at why the flag was missed
options.b: Remind him that the tool was right and that he must follow its plans
options.c: Raise it with his manager first so that it is handled formally
options.d: Let it pass, to protect the relationship with the planning team

explanation: Facts before opinions, and the person separated from the problem: looking at why the flag was missed may reveal a missing rule rather than a careless planner.
author: claude

stem: How should operators be trained on a new dispatching tool?

options.a: In a single classroom day for all shifts, a week before go-live
options.b: Through e-learning videos to be completed before go-live
options.c: By the vendor, in a demo environment with sample data
options.d: At their workstation, on real cases, shift by shift

explanation: Train at the workstation, on real cases, shift by shift. Classroom and demo training teach features; the workstation teaches the job with the tool.
author: claude

stem: Night shift gets little support after go-live and its plans drift. What helps most?

options.a: A recording of the day-shift training session for night staff
options.b: A phone hotline to the vendor's central support desk
options.c: Super-users on the night shift who coach colleagues on real cases
options.d: An email to night staff with the full user manual attached

explanation: Build super-users on every shift. A peer on site answers questions on real cases at the moment they arise; remote support and manuals do not.
author: claude

stem: Two months after go-live, the only super-user on the night shift leaves. What should the training plan have provided?

options.a: Several super-users per shift, so coaching never hinges on one person
options.b: A recording of the super-user's sessions for the next night-shift hires
options.c: A contract clause requiring the vendor to provide on-site cover
options.d: A full classroom retraining of every operator on that shift

explanation: Super-users carry training on the floor, shift by shift. Building several per shift keeps coaching alive when people move; recordings and vendor cover do not coach on real cases.
author: claude

stem: Alex plans operator training on a clean demo dataset. What does this approach miss?

options.a: The chance to collect usage data for the vendor's own model
options.b: Operators' own work and its exceptions, handled by the tool
options.c: A formal certificate that each operator can show to auditors
options.d: Coverage of every feature, which demo data shows more fully

explanation: Train on real cases at the workstation. Operators trust a tool they have seen handle their own work, exceptions included; real cases also surface missing rules early.
author: claude

stem: Plant-floor supervisors quietly keep the old routine alive despite the sponsor's support. Which group did the stakeholder map underweight?

options.a: The board, whose formal backing had already been secured
options.b: The vendor's team, who configured the tool at the start
options.c: Employee representatives, who were consulted formally
options.d: Middle management, whose daily choices shape the floor

explanation: Middle management and IT are often decisive. Supervisors decide what actually happens each shift, whatever the sponsor says.
author: claude

stem: Your stakeholder map shows a maintenance manager with high influence and low interest in the project. What follows?

options.a: Manage him closely as a key player in every project meeting
options.b: Keep him satisfied: brief him early on what touches his area
options.c: Monitor him only, with minimal effort, since interest is low
options.d: Keep him informed through the general project newsletter

explanation: On the influence-interest grid, high influence and low interest means keep satisfied. Ignoring him risks a late veto from someone who can block.
author: claude

stem: The IT manager was not consulted and now delays the tool's network access. What would most likely have prevented this?

options.a: Asking the sponsor in advance to order IT to comply
options.b: Hosting the tool outside the company network from the start
options.c: Mapping IT as a decisive stakeholder and involving it early
options.d: Choosing the tool from IT's list of preferred vendors

explanation: IT is often decisive. Mapping it early and involving it turns a likely blocker into a partner; going around it creates risk and resentment.
author: claude
